explanations.answer: To hear Him and to be healed
explanations.explanation: Ears open and hearts hurting, that's the crowd. Luke says they "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). And it doesn't stop there, friend: "those troubled by unclean spirits were healed" too (Luke 6:18). Nobody walked all the way from Tyre for nothing.

explanations.answer: To crown Him as their king
explanations.explanation: A coronation on a level place with no throne in sight? I love the ambition, baker. But Luke spells out why they came: they "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). Open ears and aching bodies. That's what they brought.

explanations.answer: To watch Him debate the Pharisees
explanations.explanation: Nobody pulled up a chair for a showdown, friend. Luke says the crowd "had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases" (Luke 6:18). They didn't travel from Judea and the coast for an argument. They came for His words and His healing.

TRUE, and what a reason! Luke says, "The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all" (Luke 6:19). All of them, baker. Not most. Not just the front row. ALL.

This one's true, friend, and it's one of my favorite lines. Luke says, "The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all" (Luke 6:19). That's why everybody was reaching. Remember my bakery when the warm batch comes out? Same reaching, WAY better reason.
You got it. Jesus says, "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). The kingdom of God, friend! Not a coupon. Not a gift card. The WHOLE kingdom belongs to them.

Powerful? Baker, Jesus flips that whole idea upside down. He says, "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). The world hands the trophy to the powerful, and Jesus opens His teaching with the poor. I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, so trust me, I like where this is going.

No red carpet in this line, friend. Jesus says, "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). Nobody has to be a big name. Look at me, I lived behind the takeout menus, and NOBODY was asking for my autograph.
Laugh! Jesus says, "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh" (Luke 6:21). Tears now, laughter later. Friend, that's a promise I'd frame and hang right over my oven.

Rule is a big word, baker, but it's not the one Jesus picks. He says, "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh" (Luke 6:21). No throne in this one. Just the people crying today laughing later, and honestly, that sounds even better to me.

Rest sounds lovely, friend, and I'd take a nap right now if the ovens would let me. But Jesus says, "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh" (Luke 6:21). It pairs up just like the hunger line before it. Hungry now, filled later. Weeping now, laughing later.

LEAP, baker! Jesus says, "Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven" (Luke 6:23). Insulted and jumping for joy at the same time? Somebody calls my stamps crooked and I sulk for a week. But Jesus gives the reason, and it's a big one: a great reward in heaven.

Hiding sounds like the natural move, friend. Believe me, I spent YEARS behind the takeout menus. But Jesus says the opposite: "Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven" (Luke 6:23). Not duck. Not hide. LEAP.

explanations.answer: Shake the dust off their feet
explanations.explanation: That phrase does show up later in Luke, baker, when Jesus sends the Twelve out to towns that won't welcome them (Luke 9:5). Here, though, He says, "Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven" (Luke 6:23). Hated and insulted, and the move is JUMPING for joy. Feet in the air, not dust off the feet.

Oh friend, that one has a twist at the end. Jesus says, "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep" (Luke 6:25). No forever laughing. It's the mirror image of the blessing back in Luke 6:21, where the ones who weep now will laugh. The laughter switches sides.

False, and nice catch! Jesus says, "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep" (Luke 6:25). Laughing now, weeping later. It's the flip side of the earlier blessing, where the ones who weep now will laugh (Luke 6:21).

False prophets, baker! Jesus says, "Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way" (Luke 6:26). Everybody clapping for you isn't always a good sign. A few lines back, the real prophets got the hate and the insults (Luke 6:22-23). The false ones got the applause.

It's not about how old they were, friend. Jesus says, "Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way" (Luke 6:26). The question is true or false. And the false ones were the crowd favorites.

Age has nothing to do with this one, friend. Jesus says, "Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way" (Luke 6:26). The warning is about getting praised the way the false prophets were. When EVERYBODY loves you, Jesus says woe, and that's worth a second look.
Enemies. Friend, I TOLD you this was the tough stretch! Jesus says, "Love your enemies" and then piles on, "do good to those who hate you" (Luke 6:27). Not tolerate. Not avoid. LOVE.

Neighbors would be the easy version, baker, and Jesus goes right past it. He says, "Love your enemies" (Luke 6:27). Then He adds, "do good to those who hate you" (Luke 6:27). The neighbor who borrows your ladder? Easy. The person who can't stand you? THAT'S the assignment.

Jesus aims somewhere a whole lot harder than the people in charge, friend. He says, "Love your enemies" and "do good to those who hate you" (Luke 6:27). Not the boss. Not the folks at the top. The people who HATE you. Whew.

True! Jesus says, "bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you" (Luke 6:28). Somebody cuts me off in traffic and my mustache is waving, and friend, it is NOT a blessing. But that's the call here: a blessing for a curse, and a prayer for mistreatment.

It's true, baker, and it's right there in the text. Jesus says, "bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you" (Luke 6:28). It's the same tough stretch that started with loving your enemies (Luke 6:27). He just keeps turning up the oven.

Your tunic, baker! Jesus says, "And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well" (Luke 6:29). Somebody grabs your coat and you hand over the shirt too? That's generosity with NO brakes.

Sandals would be a nice touch, friend, but Jesus names something else. He says, "And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well" (Luke 6:29). Cloak AND tunic. That's both layers walking out the door.

A belt would be the least of it, baker. Jesus says, "And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well" (Luke 6:29). The cloak and the tunic both. I get nervous lending out my good apron, and Jesus is talking about the shirt off your back.

explanations.answer: Do to others as you would have them do to you
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jesus says, "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31). Short, simple, and it would fit on the lid of a cookie box. Want kindness? Hand it out first.

explanations.answer: Treat others the way they have treated you
explanations.explanation: That's the rule most of us actually live by, baker, and I'm guilty too. But Jesus says, "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31). Not how they DID treat you. How you'd WANT to be treated. Big difference, especially right after He said to love your enemies (Luke 6:27).

explanations.answer: Do good to others when they have earned it
explanations.explanation: Earned? Jesus tosses the scorecard right out the window, friend. He says, "Do to others as you would have them do to you" (Luke 6:31). Nobody has to earn it first. You start with how you'd want to be treated, and you go.
True, friend. Jesus says, "Even sinners love those who love them" (Luke 6:32). Loving the people who love you back is the easy batch. ANYBODY can bake that one.

It's actually true, baker. Jesus asks, "If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you?" Then He says, "Even sinners love those who love them" (Luke 6:32). Love that only goes to people who love you back? Jesus is asking for a lot more than that.

True! Jesus says, "But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). NOTHING. No IOU, no reminder text, no awkward hint. Remember my phone charger? Like that, but on purpose.

It's true, friend, even if it sounds wild. Jesus says, "But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return" (Luke 6:35). Sinners lend expecting to be repaid in full (Luke 6:34). Jesus says lend anyway, and don't count on getting it back.

Ungrateful, baker! Jesus says the Most High "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). People who never say thank you, and He's STILL kind to them. Friend, if somebody skipped the thank you on one cookie, I'd be sulking by the oven for an hour.

Humble would be the easy word, friend, but Jesus says something way more surprising. The Most High "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). That's the Father the listeners are called to look like, right in the same verse where they're called sons of the Most High (Luke 6:35).

Faithful sounds right at first, baker, but Jesus picks a much more surprising pair of words. He says the Most High "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). The ungrateful AND the wicked! That's kindness going to people who did nothing to earn it.

Judged goes right in that first blank, friend. Jesus says, "Do not judge, and you will not be judged" (Luke 6:37). Judgment works like a boomerang. Don't throw it, and it doesn't come flying back at you.
Forgiven fills that second blank, baker. Jesus says, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). I don't hold grudges, friend, and this line is a big reason why. You let go, and you get let go.

Praised doesn't fit either blank, friend. Jesus says, "Do not judge, and you will not be judged." Then He says, "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). See the pattern? The word that goes out is the word that comes back.

Honored is a sweet word, baker, but it doesn't belong in either spot. Jesus pairs each action with its own echo. Don't judge, and you won't be judged. "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). It's a matching set, like a stamp and the print it leaves.

I like where your heart's at, friend, but Jesus keeps the words matched up. Don't judge, and you won't be judged. Forgive, and "you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37). Whatever you send out, that same word comes right back.

explanations.answer: A good measure pressed down and running over
explanations.explanation: Pressed down and RUNNING OVER, baker! Jesus says, "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap" (Luke 6:38). I pack my cookie boxes with my mustache, and even I can't get them THAT full. That's generosity spilling over the top.

explanations.answer: A small portion carefully counted out
explanations.explanation: Carefully counted? Friend, Jesus is not stingy with this picture. He says, "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap" (Luke 6:38). Pressed down so more fits, shaken so it settles, and STILL spilling over the edge.

explanations.answer: A little left over from the harvest
explanations.explanation: Leftovers? Jesus goes way bigger than that, baker. He describes "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over" poured into your lap (Luke 6:38). That's not the crumbs at the bottom of the cookie box. That's a box so full it's landing in your lap.

Measure it is, friend. Jesus says, "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Luke 6:38). Use a big scoop on others, and you get a big scoop back. Use a stingy little teaspoon, and, well, you can see where this goes.

Mercy is all over this section, baker, since Jesus just said, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36). But this blank is "measure." He says, "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Luke 6:38). Big scoop out, big scoop back.

Money's a natural guess with all this talk about lending and giving, friend. But Jesus says, "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Luke 6:38). It's the measuring cup you use on others that gets used on you. Generous scoop out, generous scoop back.

Into a pit, baker! Jesus asks, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). Two guys who can't see, one leading the other. I'm picturing the leader going, "Trust me, I know a shortcut," right before they BOTH go down.
The Jordan would at least be a soft landing, friend! But Jesus asks, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). Not a river. A pit. And the leader and the follower both go in together.

The wilderness is a fair guess for two people who can't see where they're going, baker. But Jesus asks, "Will they not both fall into a pit?" (Luke 6:39). They don't just get lost. They both fall right in.

True, friend. Jesus says, "A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40). Fully trained means looking like the one who trained you. My early stamps looked like a smudge, so I'm VERY glad nobody was training under me back then.

That one's true, baker. Jesus says a disciple is not above his teacher, "but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40). Not above the teacher, but like him. The finished student ends up looking like the one who did the training.

A BEAM, friend! Jesus talks about the speck in your brother's eye and "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41). Remember how you'd need glasses just to find that speck? The beam, you could find with your eyes closed.
A pebble would beat a speck, baker, but Jesus goes WAY bigger. He talks about "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41). A beam, a big piece of timber. Tiny thing over there, giant thing right here.

A thorn would hurt, friend, but it's still too small for this picture. Jesus sets the speck in your brother's eye next to "the beam in your own eye" (Luke 6:41). Speck versus BEAM. One you squint to see, the other you could build a porch with.
Jesus says it straight: "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). The guy's offering to fix his brother's speck with a whole beam sticking out of his own eye. "Hold still, buddy," indeed.

Jesus picks a sharper word here, baker. He says, "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). The problem is acting like the speck expert while there's a beam in your own eye. Saying one thing about your brother and missing the same thing, only bigger, in yourself.

Those words come from John the Baptist, friend, when he spoke to the crowds coming out to be baptized (Luke 3:7). Here Jesus says, "You hypocrite!" (Luke 6:42). It fits the picture perfectly. Somebody acting like he can see well enough to help, with a beam in his own eye.

True! Jesus says, "First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye" (Luke 6:42). Notice He doesn't say forget about the speck. He says beam FIRST. Clean your own counter, then go help with your neighbor's.

It's true, baker, and the order matters. Jesus says, "First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye" (Luke 6:42). Beam first, speck second. Do it the other way around and you're just poking at your brother with a beam on your face.
Fruit, friend! Jesus says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit" (Luke 6:44). You don't need a name tag on a fig tree. Just look at what's hanging off the branches.

Roots are hiding underground, baker, and you can't see them from the road. Jesus says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit" (Luke 6:44). What a tree produces tells you what it is. Same way a bakery gets known by its cookies, not its oven.

Lots of trees have leaves, friend, so leaves won't tell you much. Jesus says, "For each tree is known by its own fruit" (Luke 6:44). Figs don't come from thornbushes, and grapes don't come from brambles (Luke 6:44). What grows on the branches tells the story.

The mouth, baker! Jesus says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks" (Luke 6:45). Whatever's stored up in there comes out when you talk. It's a cookie jar. Tip it over and you find out real quick what was inside.

Hands do plenty, friend, and trust me, I use my mustache for mine. But Jesus says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks" (Luke 6:45). What fills the heart spills out in words. Your talk shows what's been stored up inside.

The eye already had its big moment with that beam, baker! Here Jesus says, "For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks" (Luke 6:45). The treasure of the heart, good or evil, comes out in what we say. Listen to somebody talk long enough and you'll smell what's baking.

This house didn't even get shaken, friend. Jesus says the torrent "crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built" (Luke 6:48). The flood came, the water hit, and NOTHING. That's what digging deep and building on the rock gets you.

False, and you caught it! Jesus says the torrent "crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built" (Luke 6:48). Not shaken. Not even a wobble. Dug down deep, foundation on the rock, and the flood got nowhere.

explanations.answer: It fell right away and was destroyed
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell" and "great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). No foundation, no chance. And that's how Jesus ends this whole teaching, with the difference between hearing His words and acting on them.

explanations.answer: It leaned hard but stayed standing
explanations.explanation: Leaning would've been a gift, friend! Jesus says, "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell" (Luke 6:49). IMMEDIATELY. And "great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). No foundation means no time to lean.

explanations.answer: It was damaged and rebuilt later
explanations.explanation: Jesus never mentions a rebuild, baker. He says, "The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell" and adds, "great was its destruction!" (Luke 6:49). Down fast and wrecked. That's the picture Jesus paints of someone who hears His words and doesn't act on them.
